title: The body is the field (13.1–13.6)
hook: the Gita began on a battlefield; chapter thirteen says the real field is you

segments.voice: Yesterday: the one dear to me. A portrait of the devoted person, and your line, free from hate, friendly to all. Did someone leave you lighter? Today, a new chapter, and a new picture. Day two hundred four.
screen: `THE ONE DEAR TO ME — FREE FROM HATE.`

segments.voice: Go all the way back to the first line of the Gita. The blind king Dhritarashtra asks: on the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus, what did my sons and the sons of Pandu do? Dharmakshetre, kurukshetre. The whole book opens on a field. Two armies, dust, chariots, a man about to break down. Twelve chapters later, chapter thirteen picks up that same word, field, kshetra, and turns it around. The field, Krishna says, isn't only out there where the armies stand. You're standing in it. You are it.
screen: `ON THE FIELD OF DHARMA.` → `TWO ARMIES, ONE FIELD.` → `THE FIELD IS YOU.`

segments.voice: Chapter thirteen opens with a definition. This body, Arjuna, is called the field. And the one who knows it, the sages call the knower of the field. Kshetra, the field. Kshetrajna, the knower of the field. Think of a farmer's field. Things grow there, weeds and wheat. Weather passes over it. Seasons change it. And standing at the edge is someone who watches it and knows it, who isn't the dirt. Then Krishna adds the line that makes this chapter famous: know me also as the knower of the field in all fields. The same knower, in every body. Hindu schools read that line differently. Advaita teachers say the knower in you and the divine knower are finally one. Ramanuja and the Vaishnava schools say the divine dwells in every knower as its inner guide, close but not identical. Both read it from the same verse. Then verses five and six list what's in the field, and the list is bigger than you'd guess. The elements. The sense of I. The intellect. The senses and the mind, and what they reach for. And then this: desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the body as a whole, awareness, steadiness. Your wanting, your not wanting, even your moods: all field. All things that grow and change and pass. Here's why that matters on an ordinary Tuesday. When anger comes up, the Gita's picture says: something is growing in the field. You can notice it from the edge. You are not only the weather. That's the word today: the body is the field.
screen: `THIS BODY IS CALLED THE FIELD.` · `THE KNOWER OF THE FIELD.` · `THE KNOWER IN ALL FIELDS.` · `EVEN DESIRE AND PAIN ARE FIELD.` · then, large: `THE BODY IS THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: Sit, and walk the edge of your own field. Notice the body first: its weight, its warmth, the places that ache. That's field. Notice the breath coming and going. Field. Notice a thought arrive, maybe a worry, maybe a wish. Field too. Then, for a moment, notice the one noticing. You don't have to name it. Just stand at the edge and watch things grow and pass. The bell holds the time.
The body is the field. Gita thirteen: the body, with its senses, desires and moods, is the field, kshetra; the one who knows it is the knower of the field.
screen: `THE BODY IS THE FIELD — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the field. Today, when a strong feeling rises, say quietly to yourself: the field. Something is growing. Then watch it from the edge for one breath. Day two hundred four.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often use Gita 13's field and knower of the field (kshetra and kshetrajna) in meditation and study, as a way of noticing the body and mind as something known, and asking who the knower is.

match.prompt: the field and its knower — tap the pairs.
pairs: the Gita's first word: the field of dharma

myth: in Gita 13 the field includes only the physical body
verses 5–6 add the mind, the sense of I, desire, aversion, pleasure and pain.
the Gita's very first verse names a field
dharmakshetre kurukshetre: on the field of dharma, the field of the Kurus.
every Hindu school reads 'the knower in all fields' the same way
Advaita reads the knowers as finally one; Ramanuja's school reads the divine as the inner guide of each.

fork.setup: anger flares in you at work. using chapter thirteen's picture, what is the anger?
options: a sign you've failed at the practice.
fork.reveal: something in the field. the Gita lists desire, aversion, pleasure and pain as field, known by the knower at the edge.

original.note: Sanskrit: kshetra, field; the same word as in Kurukshetra, the battlefield where the Gita is spoken.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Gita's field is the battlefield.
what it means: chapter thirteen says the body and mind are the field, and there's a knower of the field.
what a scholar hears: kshetra and kshetrajna; some editions open chapter 13 with an extra verse (Arjuna's question), so 13.1 in one edition is 13.2 in another.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 13.1–13.2 (the field and the knower of the field; the knower in all fields)

notes: All verses paraphrased. Verse numbering in chapter 13 differs by edition (some include an opening verse from Arjuna); check that 13.1–13.6 matches the edition the path uses.
Check the Advaita vs Ramanuja summary of 'the knower in all fields' (13.2).
The hook uses Dhritarashtra's opening question (1.1) as the frame; the Gita is Sanjaya's report to him.
